'''''Prunella vulgaris''''', the '''common self-heal''', '''heal-all''', '''woundwort''', '''heart-of-the-earth''', '''carpenter's herb''', '''brownwort''' or '''blue curls''',<ref name=cabi/><ref>{{cite book|last1=Gray|first1=Samuel F.|title=Natural Arrangement of British Plants: According to Their Relations to Each Other, as Pointed Out by Jussieu, De Candolle, Brown &c... vol 2|date=1821|publisher=Baldwin, Cradock and Joy|page=389 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TDc-AAAAcAAJ&pg=PA389|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Lust|first1=John|title=The Herb Book: The Most Complete Catalog of Herbs Ever Published|date=2014|publisher=Courier Corporation|location=USA|isbn=978-0-486-79478-5|page=399|edition=Dover republication|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YsfAAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA399}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Fisher|first1=Robert|title=The English Names of Our Commonest Wild Flowers ... |date=1932 |publisher=T. Buncle & Company|page=195|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4nlFAAAAMAAJ&q=prunella++%22brownwort%22|language=en}}</ref> is an [[herbaceous]] [[flowering plant]] in the mint family ([[Lamiaceae]]).

==Etymology==
''Prunella'' is derived from 'Brunella', a word which is itself a derivative, taken from "{{Lang|de|die Bräune}}", the [[German language|German]] name for [[diphtheria]], which ''Prunella'' was historically used to cure.<ref name="gledhill">Gledhill, David (2008). "The Names of Plants". Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback).  pp 316, 404</ref> ''Vulgaris'' means 'usual', 'common', or 'vulgar'.<ref name="gledhill" />

Self-heal and heal-all refer to its uses in traditional medicine.

==Description==
[[File:Prunella vulgaris-flowers.jpg|thumb|left|Closeup of flowers]]
''Prunella vulgaris'' grows {{convert|5-30|cm|in|abbr=on}} high,<ref>Clapham, A.R., Tutin, T.G. and Warburg, E.F. 1968. p. 347. ''Excursion Flora of the British Isles''. Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-04656-4}}</ref> with creeping, square-ish, reddish stems branching at the leaf axils.<ref name=USDA /> The opposite [[Leaf|leaves]] are lance-shaped or ovate, entire, and sometimes reddish at the tip. The leaf dimensions are {{convert|1.5-6|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|0.6-2.5|cm|in|abbr=on}} broad.<ref name="FoC">{{cite web |title=Prunella vulgaris |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200020053 |website=Flora of China |publisher=Science Press & Missouri Botanical Garden |access-date=10 January 2026}}</ref> Each leaf has 3-7 veins that shoot off the middle vein to the margin. The [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] are generally short, but can be up to {{convert|5|cm|in|abbr=on}} long.<ref>{{cite book |last=Duke |first=James |chapter=Prunella vulgaris |title=Handbook of Edible Weeds |publisher=CRC |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-8493-2946-3 |page=158 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rVrteo-8cI0C&pg=PA158}}</ref>

[[File:Kleine Braunelle, Blüte.jpg|thumb]]

The flowers grow in tight, terminal clusters, forming a spike; immediately below the inflorescence is a pair of [[sessile (botany)|sessile]] [[bracts]] on either side like a collar. The purple (sometimes white) [[corolla (botany)|corollas]] are two-lipped and tubular. The upper lip forms a hood, and the lower lip forms a cup with a fringed margin. Flowers bloom at different times depending on climate and other conditions, but mostly in summer (from June to August in the USA).<ref name="FoC"/><ref name=USDA>{{cite web |url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/charProfile?symbol=PRVU |title=Conservation Plant Characteristics for ''Prunella vulgaris'' L. (common selfheal) |work=Plants Database |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture}}</ref>

Self-heal propagates both by seed and vegetatively by [[stolons]] that root at the nodes.<ref>{{cite book |last1=DiTomaso |first1=Joseph M. |last2=Healy |first2=Evelyn A. |title=Weeds of California and Other Western States, Volume 1 |publisher=ANR |year=2007 |isbn=978-1-879906-69-3 |page=884 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=REZnaLndgoAC&pg=PA884}}</ref>

There are two described varieties of ''Prunella vulgaris'': ''var. vulgaris'' and var. ''lanceolata.'' <ref>{{Cite web|title=Calflora: Plant Search|url=https://www.calflora.org/cgi-bin/specieslist.cgi?where-genus=Prunella|access-date=2020-07-22|website=www.calflora.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Prunella vulgaris key to species, Jepson eFlora|url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_keys.php?key=39963|access-date=2020-07-22|website=ucjeps.berkeley.edu}}</ref>

Sometimes it hybridises with ''[[Prunella laciniata|P. laciniata]]'', the result known as ''[[Prunella × intermedia|P. × intermedia]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |date=2015-03-03 |first1=Vedran |last1=Šegota |first2=Antun |last2=Alegro |first3=Anja |last3=Rimac |first4=Renata |last4=Šoštarić |first5=Zorana |last5=Sedlar |first6=Ljiljana |last6=Borovečki-Voska |first7=Behija |last7=Salkić |title=Nova nalazišta hibrida roda Prunella L. u Hrvatskoj |pages=4–6 |url=https://hrcak.srce.hr/135730 |journal=Glasnik Hrvatskog botaničkog društva |eissn=1848-8102 |volume=3 |issue=1 |language=hr |trans-title=New Find Sites of Hybrids of the Genus Prunella L. in Croatia}}</ref>

==Habitat==
''Prunella vulgaris'' is a perennial herb native in [[Europe]], [[Asia]], [[Africa]], and [[North America]], and is common in most temperate climates.<ref name="cabi">{{cite web|url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/116556|title=''Prunella vulgaris'' (self-heal)|publisher=CABI|date=2019-11-19|access-date=2020-07-21}}</ref> 

''Prunella vulgaris'' can spread aggressively through creeping stolons and roots, forming dense mats that can displace other plants. Because of its ability to outcompete other desirable vegetation, it can become weedy in lawns and damp shady locations.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - The University of Texas at Austin |url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=prvu |access-date=2025-07-06 |website=www.wildflower.org}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Young-Mathews |first=Annie |date=2012 |title=Plant fact sheet for lance selfheal (Prunella vulgaris ssp. lanceolata). |url=https://plants.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/factsheet/pdf/fs_prvul2.pdf |access-date=6 July 2025 |website=USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Corvallis Plant Materials Center, Corvallis, OR.}}</ref> ''Prunella vulgaris'' is listed in ''Weeds of the Northeast'' and ''Weeds of the Great Plains''.<ref name=":1" /> It was introduced to many countries in the 1800s and has become [[Invasive species|invasive]] in the [[Pacific Islands]], including [[Australia]], [[New Zealand]], and [[Hawaii]].<ref name="cabi" /><ref>PIER, 2016. Honolulu, USA: HEAR, University of Hawaii. [http://www.hear.org/pier/index.html Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk]</ref> In [[Ireland]], it is generally abundant.<ref name="Parnell">Parnell, J. and Curtis, T. 2012. ''Webb's An Irish Flora.'' Cork University Press. {{ISBN|978-185918-4783}}</ref><ref>Scannell, M.P. and Synnott, D.M. 1972 ''Census Catalogue of the Flora of Ireland.'' Dublin Stationery Office</ref> It also grows in [[Kashmir]] where it is known as ''kalyuth'' and used as a [[decoction]] to wash and bathe in order to relieve muscle pain.<ref name="kalyuth">{{Cite journal|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10496475.2018.1564950?scroll=top&needAccess=true&journalCode=whsm20|doi=10.1080/10496475.2018.1564950|title=Ethnobotanical Survey of Daksum Forest Range of Anantnag District, Jammu and Kashmir, India|year=2019|last1=Fayaz|first1=Mufida|last2=Jain|first2=Ashok K.|last3=Bhat|first3=Musadiq Hussain|last4=Kumar|first4=Amit|journal=Journal of Herbs, Spices & Medicinal Plants|volume=25|pages=55–67|s2cid=92152206|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

It grows on roadsides, gardens, waste-places,<ref name="Parnell" /> and woodland edges, and usually in basic and neutral soils.<ref name="USDA" /><ref name="Foster-2002-p231">{{Cite book |last1=Foster |first1=Steven |last2=Hobbs |first2=Christopher |chapter=Self-heal, Heal-All |title=A Field Guide to Western Medicinal Plants and Herbs |publisher=Houghton Mifflin Harcourt |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-395-83806-8 |page=231 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tg_bPUzhJ9oC&pg=PT231}}</ref>  

The conspicuous flowers are a favorite of bumblebees and butterflies.<ref name=":1" />  ''Prunella vulgaris'' is a host species for the larvae of the  Clouded sulphur butterfly, ''[[Colias philodice]]''.<ref name=":0" />

==Uses==
[[File:Common self-heal (Prunella vulgaris) -- leaf.JPG|thumb|''P. vulgaris'' var ''lanceolata'']]
''Prunella vulgaris'' is edible.<ref name="cabi" /> The young leaves and stems can be eaten raw in salads; the plant as a whole can be boiled and eaten as a [[leaf vegetable]]; and the aerial parts of the plant can be powdered and brewed in a cold infusion to make a beverage.<ref name="cabi" /><ref name="washington-college">{{Cite web |title=Selfheal - Prunella vulgaris |url=https://www.washcoll.edu/learn-by-doing/food/plants/lamiaceae/prunella-vulgaris.php |access-date=2023-04-12 |website=www.washcoll.edu}}</ref><ref name="eatweeds">{{Cite web |last=Harford |first=Robin |date=2019-08-23 |title=Selfheal |url=https://www.eatweeds.co.uk/selfheal-prunella-vulgaris |access-date=2023-04-12 |website=EATWEEDS |language=en-GB}}</ref>

This plant was used as a traditional medicine by the indigenous peoples of North America.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fagan |first=Damian |title=Wildflowers of Oregon: A Field Guide to Over 400 Wildflowers, Trees, and Shrubs of the Coast, Cascades, and High Desert |publisher=[[FalconGuides]] |year=2019 |isbn=978-1-4930-3633-2 |location=Guilford, CT |page=172 |oclc=1073035766}}</ref> The [[Quileute]], [[Quinault Indian Nation|Quinault]], and [[Coast Salish]] in the [[Pacific Northwest]] extracted juice from the plant which was used as a topical treatment for boils. The [[Nuxalk]] boiled the entire plant to make a weak tea. The [[Nlaka'pamux]] drink a cold infusion of the whole plant as a common beverage.<ref name="Meuninck-2008-p41">{{cite book |last=Meuninck |first=Jim |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zz_mk5A2jSEC&pg=PA41 |title=Medicinal Plants of North America: A Field Guide |publisher=[[Globe Pequot Press]] |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-7627-4298-1 |page=41}}</ref>

The herb, which is called {{lang|zh-Latn|xia ku cao}} ({{wikt-lang|zh|夏枯草}}) in Chinese, is used in [[traditional Chinese medicine]] to treat dizziness, red eyes, dry cough, and dermatitis and boils.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-03-04 |title=Chinese Medicine Specimen Database |url=http://libproject.hkbu.edu.hk/was40/detail?record=1&channelid=35734&searchword=Prunella+vulgaris&sortfield=+name_chi_sort |access-date=2022-05-29 |website= |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304204905/http://libproject.hkbu.edu.hk/was40/detail?record=1&channelid=35734&searchword=Prunella+vulgaris&sortfield=+name_chi_sort |archive-date=4 March 2016 }}</ref> It is also a main ingredient in several [[Lingnan culture|herbal teas in southern China]], including commercial beverages such as [[Wong Lo Kat]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Wong Lo Kat Chinese Herbal Tea (Ingredients List) |url=https://shop.waiyeehong.com/drinks/soft-drinks/single-drinks/single-canned-drinks/wong-lo-kat-chinese-herbal-tea-1 |website=Wai Yee Hong |access-date=25 July 2020}}</ref>

==Phytochemicals==
[[Phytochemical]]s include [[betulinic acid]], <small>D</small>-[[camphor]], <small>D</small>-[[fenchone]], [[cyanidin]], [[delphinidin]], [[hyperoside]], [[manganese]] (not a phytochemical), [[lauric acid]], [[oleanolic acid]], [[rosmarinic acid]], [[myristic acid]], [[rutin]], [[linoleic acid]], [[ursolic acid]], [[beta-sitosterol]], [[lupeol]], and [[tannin]]s.<ref name="Khare-2007-p103">{{cite book |last=Khare |first=C.P. |title=Indian Medicinal Plants: An Illustrated Dictionary |publisher=Springer |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-387-70637-5 |page=103 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gMwLwbUwtfkC&pg=PA103}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Duke |first1=James A. |last2=Beckstrom-Sternberg |first2=Stephen M. |title=Handbook of Medicinal Mints (Aromathematics): Phytochemicals and Biological Activities |publisher=CRC |year=2001|isbn=978-0-8493-2724-7 |page=222 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ygJeMWHCS-EC&pg=PA222}}</ref>
